questions.q: Classify: 'She was ill, but she attended the exam.'
questions.a: Compound — 'but' is a coordinator joining two equal clauses. A wrong answer 'complex' reveals the count-only classifier — two clauses does not mean complex.

questions.q: Classify: 'Although she was ill, she attended the exam.'
questions.a: Complex — 'although' subordinates the first clause. Same meaning as the previous item, different grammar — the joiner decides the class.

questions.q: 'It rained, we stayed home.' — which structure is this?
questions.a: None — it is a comma splice (error). Needs 'so' (compound), 'because' flipped (complex), or a full stop. A wrong answer calling it compound shows the comma-power misconception.

questions.q: A complex sentence attaches a dependent clause to a main clause with a ______ (because/when/although) — one leans on the other.
Fill in the blank: Sentences multiply their verbs in two legal ways: a compound sentence joins two ______ clauses with a coordinator (and/but/or/so) — equals side by side.
Fill in the blank: Equal boxes vs leaning boxes: 'I was tired, AND I slept' — ______, two equals. 'BECAUSE I was tired, I slept' — complex, the reason leans on the result.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student distinguishes compound from complex by identifying the joiner type, and converts simple pairs into both structures.
